findings.element: state=day — the wedding morning (.b-field on [data-state="day"]) and its one control, summary.b-behindSummary
findings.problem: The past was rebuilt and it is good: driven at 390 the disclosure opens onto a real rail, ticks, mono dates, at two pixels a day, headed "days back". The forward half of the day was not touched. Measured at 390x844 the morning still holds 199 characters of text, one focusable node, and a .b-field 698px tall inside an 844px screen. "Happening now" resolves to two words, "Wedding day", and stays byte-identical from 00:00 to 23:59; there is no running order, no next thing, and no time of day anywhere on the screen. The claim that the day now names every moment dated on it cannot be tested, because the fixture puts exactly one moment on 3 October — so the assertion is unfalsifiable and the screen a guest actually gets is a single line. The one control makes it worse: pressing the disclosure grows the document from 844 to 1444, leaves scrollY at 0, and puts the last of the nine revealed rows at 1191px, 347px below the fold with no cue that it continues. So on the flagship morning the audience gets a poster, and the only thing they can do on it is open a list whose end is off-screen. Every other guest state hands the reader something to travel down.
findings.fix: Two changes. First, give the fixture a real wedding day — at least six moments dated 2026-10-03 carrying times (guests arrive 13:30, ceremony 14:00, photographs 15:15, dinner 17:30, speeches 19:00, first dance 21:00) — so the day state renders the object it claims to render and every seat can grade it. Second, render those moments as .b-item rows in the existing list above the "How you got here" block, with .b-measureHead reading "now" instead of "days away", each row carrying its time in the count's mono slot in place of a day count, exactly one row marked data-now="true" at full ink with the indigo tick, rows after it at .b-title ink and rows before it at --fore-62, with no control on any of them. Then, on the disclosure's toggle event, when the revealed block's bottom exceeds the viewport, scrollIntoView the block's first row so it sits under the summary, on the 0.22s step and set to auto under prefers-reduced-motion, leaving focus on the summary where it already correctly stays.

findings.element: state=print — section.b-print, and the absence of any print geometry in master.html
findings.problem: Judged as a physical object the keepsake is not a page, it is a web column that a printer happens to cut. .b-print measures 792 x 1440px, a 1.818 aspect against A4's 1.414. Grepped across master.html, a.css, b.css and c.css there is no @page rule, no @media print block, no break-inside, no page-break, and no mm unit anywhere. Printed to A4 it is two sheets. At default browser margins sheet two carries only the "Behind you" block, the raw link and the foot — it names neither the couple nor the date, so a leaf on its own identifies nobody; sheet one, conversely, has no "Kept by Orla", no date and no way back to the plan. At zero margins, which is the setting a person picks to make a keepsake fill the paper, the 1123px page edge cuts straight through the .b-behindRow spanning 1100 to 1139 — the engagement, "We said yes", sliced in half across two sheets. The composition is wrong for paper besides: roughly 600px of the left column on sheet one is blank below "Nothing is planned until 1 August", the rail overruns 60px past "79 · Wedding day" into dead line, the day itself gets the same open tick as every ordinary row, and the only route back to the live plan is a 60-character URL a human has to transcribe by hand.
findings.fix: Give the print state a real page. Add @page { size: A4; margin: 14mm; } and size .b-print in millimetres (a 182mm x 269mm content box) rather than pixels, so what is drawn is the sheet. Set break-inside: avoid on .b-item, .b-behindRow and .b-copy so no moment is ever cut. Repeat identity on every sheet: put "Mara & Finn · Saturday 3 October 2026" in a running head at the top of each page and "Kept by Orla · Signal Timeline" in a running foot, both at the label step. Close the rail on the anchor — end the .b-measure line at the wedding-day tick with no overrun, and draw that tick filled at full ink so the day terminates the object. Then pull the sheet back to one leaf by moving the "Behind you" block into the empty lower half of the left column. Replace the printed URL string with a 24mm QR code beside a short human-readable label; the full string stays only in the accessible name.

findings.element: state=day — .b-away and its unit span inside details.b-behindDetails, against h2.b-measureHead
findings.problem: The new past rail on the wedding morning is headed "days back" and then every single row under it reads "days away". Driven at 390 with the disclosure open, the eight rows announce: "14 days away, Venue walk-through, SAT 19 SEP" / "28 days away, Final guest numbers" / "35 days away" / "42" / "56" / "63" / "168" / "274 days away". Every one of those dates is in the past. A guest reading the morning is told the venue walk-through is fourteen days away on a rail whose own heading says it is fourteen days back, and the accessible name repeats the wrong word rather than correcting it. This is the exact class the defect library names as one grammar per fact, on the one screen the whole product exists for, introduced by the very fix that was supposed to make the morning speak the product's language. The behaviour gate is not neutral here: its assertion "every row speaks its unit" tests /days away/ against every row, so the gate is currently enforcing the false word rather than catching it.
findings.fix: Bind the unit to the row's own direction rather than to the component. Where the rail is drawn with data-direction="back", render the unit as "days back" in the visible span and in the accessible name — "Venue walk-through. Saturday 19 September, 14 days back." — and keep "days away" only where the count runs toward a future date. Drop the trailing comma from the unit span while you are in it; it reads as a fragment on its own line and in the accessible name alike. Then amend the gate's row-unit assertion to test that each row's unit matches its own sign — /days (away|back)/ chosen by whether the row's date falls before or after today — so the assertion catches this class instead of certifying it.

findings.element: state=loading — section.b-field[aria-busy] and its .b-skel blocks at widths above 700px
findings.problem: At 390 the frame is exact and deserves the credit: the three skeleton blocks sit at 65/161/191 with sizes 107x86, 227x26 and 188x23, and the arriving header lands at 65/161/191 with .b-num 107x86, .b-when 26 high and .b-sub 23 high — nothing moves. At desk width the same card is drawn unchanged, and it is then wrong in both axes. Measured at 1440: the loading .b-field is 388px wide at left 526; the desk artifact it resolves into is 1178px wide at left 131. .b-who runs from left 548 to left 187 when the data lands, so the whole header the frame drew so carefully jumps 361px sideways. Vertically it drops 22px, and the hero count is under-promised by half — a 107x86 skeleton bar against a real 148px glyph measuring 164x133. The frame is honest about not inventing a measure and then dishonest about the shape and size of the one block it does draw. A reader on a laptop watches the plan's identity slide most of a card's width across the screen at the moment it becomes real.
findings.fix: Make the loading field inherit the same width and column rules as the state it resolves into rather than rendering the phone card at every width: apply the desk field's max-width and grid to [data-state="loading"] above the 701px breakpoint, so the frame's left edge is the artifact's left edge. Size the count skeleton from the display step in force at that width instead of a fixed 107x86 — 164px by 133px above 701px, 107x86 below, matching the two ends of the count's type ramp. The 22px vertical drop goes with it, because .b-who is then placed by the same rule in both states.

findings.element: the custom-property layer in master.html against the .b-* class layer in render-b.js
findings.problem: Asked whether a second product can be built from this without copying it, the answer from my lens is half yes. The material half is genuinely extractable and better than most shipped systems: a nine-stop ink ladder mirrored three ways (--ink-04 to --ink-90, --paper-*, --fore-*), a nine-name vertical ladder (--gap-hair through --gap-page), leading and tracking bound to six named roles rather than to elements (--lead-display/head/title/body/date/label and --track-* to match), three durations with exactly one --ease, and a single --focus property every ring routes through. Notes could wear that tomorrow. The behavioural half does not exist as a language at all. The real inventions here are interaction contracts: the row is the control, with its whole box as the target and its state, its mark and its accessible name as one object; one reversibility node that travels, stays silent until it has something true to say, names the change in words and returns focus to the control that made it; a stepper that states its ceiling rather than absorbing the press; an editor that is a gutter above 1280 and a sheet below without dropping focus. Every one of those is spelled as a .b--prefixed class inside direction B's own stylesheet, and the contract exists only inside the gate's assertions. A second product cannot inherit "the row is the control" from a class named .b-grab; it can only copy this file.
findings.fix: Extract a behaviour spec beside the token file — one page, four named contracts, each with its required states, its accessible-name grammar, its keyboard bindings and its focus-return rule. Row: the whole box is the target; the name carries title, date, distance and visibility; Enter opens, Escape closes and returns focus. Reversal: one node per surface, role=status, silent at rest, names the change in words, binds Ctrl/Cmd+Z, yields inside text fields, returns focus to the origin control. Step: states its ceiling in words, never moves under the pointer, holds scroll and focus through the repaint. Panel: gutter above the stated breakpoint, sheet below, opaque either way, focus preserved across the switch. Rename the classes off the direction letter to those four names so the markup carries the contract rather than the experiment's initial, and move the gate's assertions for each contract under its heading so a second product inherits the tests together with the language.

biggestWin: The owner's editing surface holds its place under every kind of disturbance, and I could not break it. Driven at 1440 with focus parked on "Move a day later", I resized to 1280, 1024, 768 and 390 and back: the editor switches from a relative gutter plate 344px wide to a fixed sheet at 1000, 744 and 366px, and at every single step focus stays on the same stepper, scrollY stays at 0, and the focused control stays inside the viewport. A press is now answered before the intent is — the row copy steps from 4% to 10% ink under the finger, on the ladder, with no reflow: the row tops are byte-identical between rest and hover. The reversibility node still names the exact change in words, its key still works, it still falls silent when there is nothing left to undo, and it still hands focus back to the control that made the change. That is the hardest thing on the whole surface, it survives the layout mode changing under it, and no other seat's finding can take it away.
